content: 1. Pilates has been shown to improve exercise tolerance in patients with non-communicable diseases (NCDs). There is moderate evidence supporting its benefits in alleviating symptoms, enhancing muscle strength, and improving health-related quality of life. However, evidence regarding its effects on vital signs, metabolic parameters, body composition, respiratory function, functional status, balance, flexibility, and social support remains limited or conflicting. Future studies with rigorous methodologies are necessary to better understand its effectiveness and to establish optimal intervention protocols. 2. Dance interventions have been studied for their effects on balance, gait, and functional mobility in adults with neurological conditions other than Parkinson’s disease. A systematic review included nine studies, which varied in methodological quality from poor to good. Participants included individuals with stroke, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, and Huntington’s disease. Dance interventions differed in frequency, type, and duration, with only one study reporting intensity. Significant improvements were observed in spatiotemporal gait parameters, Berg Balance Scale scores, Timed Up and Go test, and six-minute walk test. These changes were comparable to or exceeded those reported in studies on dance for Parkinson’s disease. Dance appears to be a feasible intervention for improving balance and mobility in this population, but further research with larger sample sizes and randomized controlled trials is needed. 3. A systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated the effects of exercise programs combining aerobic and resistance training, prescribed according to American Stroke Association guidelines, on mobility and physical activity levels in stroke survivors. Data from 499 participants were analyzed. Combined exercise programs were found to improve mobility outcomes, with high adherence and minimal adverse events reported. These programs are safe and should be prescribed alongside usual care to enhance mobility in stroke survivors. Further research is needed to explore the relationship between exercise programs and long-term behavior change to sustain physical activity levels. 4. Virtual reality (VR)-based balance training combined with tele-rehabilitation has been investigated for its feasibility and effectiveness in community-dwelling stroke survivors. Seven studies, including four randomized controlled trials, demonstrated that VR provides a motivational environment for longer and more engaging training sessions. Tele-rehabilitation offers a cost-effective alternative to therapist-supervised interventions, with comparable effects on balance and functional mobility. While evidence is still limited, this approach shows promise for improving accessibility to rehabilitation and enhancing adherence to therapy. 5. High-intensity interval training (HIIT) has been evaluated for its effectiveness in improving fitness and mobility in stroke survivors. Six studies, including three randomized controlled trials, reported significant improvements in peak oxygen consumption, 10-Meter Walk Test, and Functional Ambulation Categories compared to baseline. However, HIIT was not significantly more effective than moderate-intensity continuous exercise (MICE) for some outcomes, such as the 6-Minute Walk Test and Berg Balance Scale. Preliminary evidence suggests that HIIT may be an effective rehabilitation intervention for certain aspects of cardiorespiratory fitness and mobility post-stroke, but further research is needed. 6. Tai Chi exercise has been shown to significantly improve balance function in stroke patients. A meta-analysis of six studies reported increased Berg Balance Scale scores and reduced fall rates in the Tai Chi intervention group compared to controls. Tai Chi may enhance balance efficiency, but further research is required to confirm its effects on other outcomes, such as gait parameters and functional reach. 7. Mindful exercises, such as Tai Chi and yoga, have been found to improve sensorimotor function in the upper and lower limbs of post-stroke patients. A systematic review of 20 studies highlighted their potential benefits for gait speed, leg strength, aerobic endurance, and overall motor function. However, further investigation is needed to draw evidence-based conclusions about their effects on cognitive function and other rehabilitative outcomes. 8. Mind-body exercises, including Tai Chi and yoga, may improve mood and functional capabilities in stroke survivors. A meta-analysis of 16 randomized controlled trials demonstrated significant reductions in depression and anxiety, as well as improvements in activities of daily living and functional mobility. These exercises could serve as effective adjunct treatments, but more robust studies are needed to confirm their long-term benefits and establish standardized protocols.
